## Submission metadata

- **Conference:** Data Curation Conference 2027, Research Data Management Network, University of Basel, Thursday 14 January 2027
- **Format:** Workshop session, 75 minutes with discussion, 10:45 to 12:00, 10 to 20 participants
- **Presenter:** Lars Schöbitz
- **Discipline:** Global health engineering (water, sanitation and health)
- **Use case:** Survey and monitoring data from the water, sanitation and health sector, from the raw file to a published data package and website
- **Data curation aspect(s):** Presentation of data to humans, documentation, versioning, metadata, AI assisted curation with disclosure, sensitive data
- **Version:** Revised for the conference website on 9 November 2026 after the acceptance, with the agenda, the learning objectives and the prerequisites the organisers asked for. The version submitted on 21 October 2026 is release v1.0.0 of the repository https://github.com/Global-Health-Engineering/workshop-dcc-2027

## Abstract

Survey and monitoring data from the water, sanitation and health sector mostly lives in spreadsheets that only their owners can read. For five years, Global Health Engineering at ETH Zurich has turned such files into published data, for our own projects and, through openwashdata, for the wider sector. Versioned code processes the raw file into an analysis ready dataset with a data dictionary and machine readable metadata, packaged as an R data package, archived with a DOI, and presented on a website with documentation and plots built from the data. AI now does most of the mechanical work. We publish for machines and humans. This workshop is about the humans, who still have to discover, interpret and trust data that machines parse with ease.

In the workshop I run the workflow live, from a messy raw file to a published data package and website, with the free, open source tools washr (to build) and pkgreview (to review). A coding agent performs the mechanical steps. Participants propose documentation changes as comments on a GitHub issue and I merge them in front of the room, so every human and every AI intervention stays visible. Participants who send a dataset of their own beforehand find it published as a data package during the session and leave with a citable dataset under their name. Everyone takes home a picture of what a published dataset looks like for a human reader, the tools to get there in one sitting, and a record of how AI took part. The discussion takes up four themes the workflow raises for data curation: oversight of AI curation, disclosure of AI contributions, sensitive data, and scientific credit for data.

## Agenda (75 minutes)

1. Introduction, 10 minutes. Why we publish for humans, the workflow in one picture, the three stages of data (raw, analysis ready, final), and the links to the participants' own data packages, for everyone to explore during the live run.
2. Live run, part 1, 25 minutes. From the raw file to a documented data package with washr. The agent does the mechanical steps (folder structure, data dictionary, metadata, README). Participants post documentation changes as comments on the workshop's GitHub issue, and I merge them live, each commit naming its proposer.
3. Live run, part 2, 15 minutes. Review with pkgreview, release, DOI and website. The disclosure trail (commit trailers, prompt archive) on the repository. One or two of the participants' packages opened and compared.
4. Discussion, 20 minutes. Four themes, five minutes each. Oversight of AI curation, disclosure of AI contributions, sensitive data, scientific credit for data.
5. Take home, 5 minutes. Where the repository lives, how to run washr on your own data, who to ask.

## Learning objectives

After the workshop, participants can

- describe the stages a raw dataset passes through on its way to a published data package and website, and what a human reader needs at each stage (documentation, data dictionary, metadata, plots);
- tell which steps of data curation a coding agent can take over, which stay with the researcher, and how AI contributions are recorded so that they stay visible;
- build, document and review a data package from their own data with washr and pkgreview, and publish it with a DOI;
- weigh the four themes (oversight, disclosure, sensitive data, credit) for their own data and their own institution.

## Prerequisites

- Bring a laptop. Before the workshop, by Friday 11 December 2026, take the ten minute pre-course survey (it records your GitHub username and walks you through creating an account if you have none) and post one comment on the check-in issue of the workshop repository. The workshop website, https://rawtoweb.github.io/website/dcc-2027/, explains both steps and what an issue is. Comments on an issue are how everyone contributes during the live run. If a step fails for you, pair with a neighbour on the day.
- Optional, to run the steps yourself: install R, RStudio or Positron and the washr package. The setup guide and the sample dataset are on the workshop website from 5 January 2027.
- Optional, to leave with a published data package: submit a dataset through the form on the workshop website by Friday 11 December 2026, either your own data (a CSV or Excel file with a few lines on its origin) or a published dataset under CC BY 4.0 or CC0 that you pick. The data must hold no personal data. I build a data package from it before the conference, you review it, and it is published with a DOI, with you as author (own data) or contributor (a dataset you picked).
